To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

giving food before a session increased the rate of responding for water and decreased the rate of responding and time on the lever for food; giving water before a session had opposite effects on the rate of responding; giving both food and water increased the rate of food and water consumption and increased the rate of water and decreased the time on the lever and rate of responding for food.
the effects of prefeeding on concurrent variable-intervals with water reinforcement and the effects of prewatering on concurrent variable-intervals with food reinforcement are additive.

the relative reinforcing strength of food and water in a concurrent variable-interval schedule is affected by the availability of food and water before the session, and that the availability of food or water before a session affects the amount of food and water consumed during the session.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of food and water deprivation on concurrent variable-intervall schedules of reinforcement.
the effects of pre-session access to food or water on concurrent variable-intervals schedules.
the effects of concurrent schedules of reinforcement on the behavior and physiology of rats.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of prefeeding and/or prewatering on concurrent variable-intervals schedules are complex and depend on the amount of prefeeding and the amount of prewatering.
prefeeding decreased response rates and per cent time in food component and increased response rates and percent time in water component.
the effects of prefeeding and of prewatering on concurrent performance depend on the relative magnitudes of these variables and on the relative magnitude of the concurrent schedule values.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
food is a more effective reinforcer for lever pressing than water.
food and water are both reinforcing, that they have different motivational properties, and that the effects of prefeeding and/or prewatering are complex.
the relative reinforcing efficacy of food and water is determined by their relative availability before a session.
The main takeaway from our work is that
concurrent variable-interval food-water schedules may be useful for studying how food and water affect motivation.
concurrent VI food and water schedules can provide an excellent tool for studying the effects of prefeeding on concurrent responding.

prefeeding and pre-watering effects on response allocation and response rates are similar to those found with other reinforcers, but they are opposite to those found with food and water when they are available during a session.
